newsitem.title: INDIA: FULL TEXT-RBI's monetary policy for second half '96/97.
newsitem.headline: FULL TEXT-RBI's monetary policy for second half '96/97.

text.p: Following is the full text of the Reserve Bank of India's monetary policy for second half 1996/97 (April-March), announced on Saturday:
REAL SECTOR DOWN BUT AGRICULTURE SEEN BETTER
1. The real sector of the Indian economy after having grown strongly for the past two years has shown in the current year some deceleration particularly in the industrial sector.

However, agriculture is expected to perform much better and this will have a favourable impact on industrial production with some lag. On the whole, the Indian economy in 1996-97 should perform more or less as in the past two years. The monetary and credit scenario presents a mixed picture. Monetary growth so far in the credit scenario presents a mixed picture.

Monetary growth so far in the current year has been on the targeted growth path of 15.5 to 16.0 percent. The deposit growth has been strong especially in contrast to the situation that prevailed last year in the corresponding period. Credit growth has slackened evh was around 5 percent in the early months of the current financial year has moved up to 6.3 percent on an year-on-year basis.
These are some developments which need to be kept in view while formulating the monetary and credit policy for the second half of the year.
FOODGRAINS OUTPUT TO SURPASS PREVIOUS HIGH

2. The rate of growth in real GDP in 1995-96 which was estimated at 7 percent is now placed at around 6.2 percent with the latest data on agricultural performance showing practically no value addition. In the current year, agricultural performance showing practically no value addition. In the current year, agriculture is likely to record a 3-to-4 percent growth.

Foodgrains production is expected to surpass the previous peak of 191.1 million tonnes reached in 1994-95. Industrial production which was the main driving force behing the real GDP growth in 1995-96 has shown signs of slackness. During the first quarter of the current financial year (April to June 1996), the index of industrial production recorded a growth of 8.5 percent which is much lower than the growth of 14.7 percent recorded in the first quarter of 1995-96.

However, within industrial production, the manufacturing sector recorded a growth of 10.4 percent. The deceleration in the growth rate is mostly attributed to declines in the growth rates in mining and electricity. These sectors recorded very low growth of 3.6 percent to 2.2 percent respectively. However, with good rains, the generation of electricity should show improvement during the second half of the year.

The improved performance of agriculture should also have a favourable effect on industrial growth in the second half of the year. Thus, on the whole, while the industrial growth will be lower than what it was in the previous year, it could nevertheless be expected to be around 9-to-10 percent.
INFLATION

3. Inflation rate as measured by the wholesale price index was 6.3 percent (provisional data) on year-on-year basis during the week ended September 28, 1996 as compared with that of 8.8 percent during the comparable week of the previous year.

The increase in the wholesale price index from April 1, 1996 till September 28,1996 has been 5.8 percent. It should be our endeavour to see that the inflation rate remains between 6 and 7 percent during the year as a whole.
MONETARY AND CREDIT DEVELOPMENTS

4. Monetary and credit developments during the first half of the current financial year provide a mixed trend. Broad money (M3) showed an increase of Rs. 37,578 crore (6.2 percent) (one crore=10 million rupees) as compared with that of Rs. 23,327 crore (4.4 percent) during the coparable period of 1995-96, mainly on account of a sizeable increase in the time deposits with banks.

Growth in currency with the public, however, has been subdued during this period. Reserve money recorded a negative growth of Rs. 10,426 crore (5.4 percent) during the current financial year so f, in contrast with the increase of Rs. 5,379 crore (3.2 percent) in the comparable period of the previous year.

This was mainly on account of a pronounced decline of Rs. 13,816 crore in Resevce Bank's claims on scheduled commercial banks due primarily to negligible utilisation of export credit refinance by banks since July 1996.

Net foreign exchange assets of the RBI increased sharply by Rs. 7,559 crore during the current financial year so far upto September 27,1996 in contrast with a decline of Rs. 2,857 crore during the comparable period of 1995-96.

On the other hand, the increase in net RBI credit of central government by Rs. 3,801 crore during the current financial year so far was less than one half of the increase of Rs. 8,714 crore during the same period of 1995-96. Reserve money growth adjusted for the changes in the CRR, during the current fiancial year so far was negative at Rs. 1,126 crore (0.6 percent) in contrast with an increase in Rs. 5,379 crore (3.2 percent) during the comparable period of 1995-96.
FOOD CREDIT FALLS

5. While aggregate deposits of scheduled commercial banks recorded a pronounced increase of Rs. 27,926 crore (6.4 percent) during the first of the current financial year (i.e., from march 29 to September 27,1996) as compared with Rs. 11,740 crore (3.0 percent) during the corresponding period of 1995-96, there has been a decline in bank credit.
Food credit declined by Rs. 1,356 crore in contrast with the modest increase of Rs. 332 crore during the first half of 1995-96 due to the lower than envisaged level of procurement of wheat.

Non-food bank credit of scheduled commercial banks declined by Rs. 1,710 crore (0.7 percent) during the first half of the current financial year in contrast with an increase of Rs. 9,897 crore (5.0 percent) during the comparable period of the previous year.
INVESTMENT BY COMMERCIAL BANKS

6. Investments by scheduled commercial banks in government securities in the first of the current financial year were higher by Rs. 13,074 crore as against Rs. 6,178 crore in the corresponding period of the previous year.
As against the budgetted gross market borrowing of Rs. 35,294 crore of the central government in 1996-97, Rs. 27,702 crore has been raised in the current financial year upto October 11, 1996.

These trends show that the central government would be able to raise the remainder of the budgetted borrowing programme in the coming months of the year without causing any upward pressure on interest rates.
INTEREST RATES SOFTENING
7. Reflecting the improvement in the overall liquidity position in the financial system, there has been some softening in market interest rates.
The inter-bank call market rates ruled generally in the range of 10.00-11.25 percent in the first quarter of 1996-97. By July 1996, they declined sharply to as low as 0.10-3.00 percent.
After staying at such historically low levels for about a fortnight, call rates began to move upward, and have ruled in the range of 5.00-10.95 percent through Sepember 1996.

In October so far, the rates have been rulling in the range of 6.00-10.00 percent. The typical interest rates on Certificate of Deposit (CDs) and Commercial Paper (CP) have also moved down since April 1996. The typical rate of interest on CDs of 3 months and 1 year maturity declined from 17.0-19.0 percent and 18.0-19.0 percent in early April 1996 to 11.5-13.0 percent and to 13.0 percent respectively at end-August 1996.

The typical rates of discount on CPs also moved down from 18.00-25.25 percent in April 1996 to 13.00-14.25 percent by end-September 1996. The yields on Treasury Bills and dated government securities have also tended to drift downward. The 91-day auction treasury bill which gave yields about 12.97 percent at the beginning of the year now yield little over 10.0 percent.

The yields on 364-day treasuy bills moved down from 13.12 percent at the beginning of April 1996 to around 12.61 percent by October 11,1996. The 10-year bonds fetched a coupon rate of 13.85 percent as against the 14.0 percent in 1995-96. In the forex market, forward premia have come down since July 1996.
LENDING RATES REMAIN HIGH

8. Notwithstanding the downward movement in certain market rates of interest, the lending rates of banks have remained relatively high, with reductions in Prime Lending Rates (PLRs) being confined to only a few public sector banks.

The PLR of some banks which ruled at 16.5 percent from the November 1995 to mid-July 1996 was brought down to 16.0 percent under the impact of a sharp increase in lendable resources prompted by cuts in CRR.

Due to reductions in CRR since November 1995, there was a total release of resources to the tune of Rs. 16,825 crore - Rs. 7,525 crore during the second half of 1995-96 and Rs. 9,300 crore during 1996-97 (upto July 1996). In September-October 1996, a few banks reduced the PLR to 15.5 percent but this was not systemwide.

Irrespective of the PLR, banks also continue to charge very high rates of interest. In Septmber 1996 the maximum lending rate charged was as high as PLR plus over 4 percent in respect of 47 banks. In the case of only 18 banks the maximum interest rate charged was PLR plus upto 4 percent.
DEVELOPMENT IN THE EXTERNAL SECTOR

9. The current account deficit which was estimated at 1.7 percent of GDP in 1995-96 is expected to be around 2 percent of GDP in 1996-97. In the five months of April-August of the current financial year, the trade deficit was limited. Export growth in dollar terms was 9.8 percent, while imports increased only by 4.7 percent. Non-oil imports declined. There is a strong need for improving exports and ensuring imports to sustain growth momentum.
FOREIGN CURRENCY ASSETS RISE

10. Foreign currency assets increased from $17,025 million at end-March 1996 to $18,429 million by the end of September 1996. There has been further accretion to foreign currency assets since then to reach $18,813 million as on October 17, 1996. It should be possible without loss of foreign currency assets to meet all repayment obligations during the year.
STABLE EXCHANGE RATE

11. The foreign exchange market remained fairly stable during the current financial year so far. The rupee-dollar rate moved within the range of Rs.34.22-35.65 to $1 in the first half of the year. The broad objective of exchange rate policy will continue to be to ensure a stable real exchange rate. The stability of the external value of the rupee is linked to domestic price stability and as such monetary policy has to ensure that inflationary pressures are contained within limits.
STANCE OF MONETARY POLICY

12. We have to continue to pursue the two basic objective of monetary policy viz., price stability and adequate supply of bank credit to the productive sectors of the economy. The M3 growth target of 15.5-16.0 percent should enable us to meet the twin objectives. As such, the working estimate of the increase in aggregate deposits of Rs. 68,000 crore (15.7 percent) during 1996-97 is retained.

Food credit is estimated to increase by Rs. 1,100 crore during the third quarter (i.e. October-December 1996) and decline by Rs. 700 crore during the fourth quarter (January-March 1997), showing a net increases of Rs. 400 crore in the second half of 1996-97.
LOANS TO SMALL-SCALE FIRMS

13. The decline in non-food credit during 1996-97 so far needs to be corrected. Besides exports, banks need to pay particular attention to agriculture and small-scale industries. Banks have already been advised to increase the disbursements for agriculture by 25 percent during the current year. Banks must take appropriate action to reach this goal.

In the case of small-scale industries, public sector banks were required to open 100 SSI specialised branches in 85 identified districts during 1995-96. As against this target, banks have operationalised 136 branches during 1996-97.

There are continuing complaints about the lack of adequate credit for small scale industrial units. Banks need to take note of this and evolve appropriate measures to improve the flow of credit to small-scale industries. On the whole, banks must overcome the hesitancy to lend funds even as they adhere to prudential norms.
CHANGES IN MEASURES
14. It is against this background, I am announcing the following measures:
(a) Cash Reserve Ratio

Under Section 42(1) of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, scheduled commercial banks (excluding regional rural banks) are, at present, required to maintain with the Reserve Bank of India, a cash reserve ratio (CRR) of 12.0 percent of their net demand and time liablities (excluding liabilities subject to a zero CRR prescription).

Consistent with the medium term objectives and on a review of the current monetary and credit situation, it has been decided to reduce the cash reserve ratio. Accordingly, the CRR to be maintained by scheduled commercial banks (excluding regional rural banks) is being reduced by two percentage points from 12.0 percent to 10.0 percent in four phases of 0.5 percentage point each as set out below.

Giving effect to the one percentage point reduction in CRR during January 1997 is, however, contingent on the monetary and price situation at that time. Each percentage point reduction in CRR would enhance the lendable resources by about Rs. 4,275 crore and enable the banks to augment their earnings.
A notification of this change would be send to banks seperately.
(b) Export Credit Refinance

Total export credit refinance limits of scheduled commercial banks for the fortnight ended September 27, 1996 were Rs. 11,377 crore and average utilisation during this fortnight was Rs. 1,587 crore forming 13.9 percent of limits.

As a move towards further rationalisation of CRR and refinance to banks, with effect from the fortnight beginning November 9, 1996, scheduled commercial banks will be provided export credit refinance to the extent of 20 percent of the outstanding export credit eligible for refinance (instead of 45 percent at present) upto the level of such credit as on February 16, 1996 plus 100 percent of the increase in outstanding export credit eligible for refinance over the level as on February 16, 1996.

The rate of interest on export credit refinance will continue to be at 11.0 percent per annum. In view of the low utilisation of export credit refinance during the recent period, and the release of resources through reduction in CRR, there would be adequate resources available for financing export credit.
Detailed operating instructions would be issued seperately.
(c) Target for Export Credit

With a view to bringing about a significant and enduring increases in export credit and ensuring that the banking system meets the genuine credit requirements of the export sector fully and expeditiously, scheduled commercial banks were advised in November 1992 to endeavour to reach a level of export credit equivalent to 10.0 percent of each bank's net bank credit.

During the current financial year so far upto September 27, 1996, aggregate export credit declined by Rs. 4,464 crore (14.1 percent) to Rs. 27.294 crore resulting in a ratio of banks' aggregate export credit to net bank credit of 10.9 percent.

In view of the above and recognising the paramount need to promote exports, the target for export credit of scheduled commercial banks is being increased from the present 10.0 percent of each bank's net bank credit to 12.0 percent of each bank's net bank credit.

This revised target will have to be reached by end-March 1997. The progress of banks in attaining the stipulated target will be closely monitored. Banks which had already attained a higher ratio of export credit than the target should ensure that there is no fall in the ratio. Failure to achieve the stipulated level of export credit target could invite bank-specific policy responses.
Communication of this changes is being sent to banks seperately.
(d) Interest Rates on Term Deposits

At present, interest rates on domestic term deposits of scheduled commercial banks (excluding Regional Rural Banks) are subject to a prescription of not exceeding 11.0 percent per annum for maturity of 30 days and upto 1 year. For maturity of over 1 year, banks are free to fix their own interest rates.

It has been decided to reduce effective from October 21, 1996 the deposit rates for maturity of 30 days and upto 1 year by one percentage point for not exceeding 11.0 percent per annum to not exceeding 10.0 percent per annum.

Banks should continue to obtain the prior approval of their respective Boards for the deposit rates they will be offering on deposits of maturity of over 1 year. At any point of time, individual banks should adopt uniform rates at all their branches and for all customers. The revised term deposits rates will apply only to fresh deposits and renewal of maturing deposits. The existing and the revised term deposit rates are set out below:

(e) Rationalisation of Interest Rates on Post-Shipment Rupee Export Credit

A present, interest rate on post-shipment rupee export credit upto 90 days is prescribed at 13.0 percent per annum. Banks have the freedom to fix their own interest rates on post-shipment rupee export credit for over 90 days and upto 180 days from the date of advance.

Banks are also free to determine the interest rates on export credit beyond six months from the date of shipment. The exporters have represented that the benefit of prescribed interest rate at 13.0 percent per annum is denied even for a period upto 90 days in case of the total period of the bill including transit period is beyond 90 days.

There is, therefore, a need for rationalisation of interest rates on export credit. Keeping this in view, it has been decided that effective October 21, 1996 for post-shipment rupee export credit for the period beyond 90 days and upto six months, banks should charge interest rate of 15 percent per annum.

In respect of post-shipment credit beyond 90 days, the higher rate of interest will apply only for the period beyond 90 days and not from the date of advance. This measure would reduce the effective cost of credit to the exporters and make exports more competitive. (f) Prime Lending Rate

At present, scheduled commercial banks are free to determine their own lending rates on their advances with limits of over Rs.2 lakh. As a result of reductions in reserve requirements, the proportion of pre-emptive resources of banks has substantially been brought down. This in turn has improved the average return on funds. Banks need to pass on at least part of the gains to the borrowers.

Extremely high interest rates would affect the viability of the borrowers' capacity to repay. Besides, they would be unsustainable as they may eventually result in an increase in the non-performing assets (NPA) of the banks. In the light of the package of measures announced today, it is expected that banks would reduce their Prime Lending Rates appropriately.

It is also observed that a number of banks are charging lending rates far higher than PLR on a significant portion of bank credit to borrowers with credit limits of over Rs. 2 lakh. Credibility of the PLR is lost if the actual interest rates charged by the banks are sharply higher than the PLR.

It has, therefore, been decided that banks, along with the announcement of their PLR, should also announce the maximum spread over the Prime Lending Rate for all advances other than consumer credit. Banks should obtain the aproval of their respective Boards for fixation of maximum spread over the Prime Lending Rate.
A separate communication will be sent to banks.
(g) Selective Credit Controls

Presently, bank advances against pulses, 'other foodgrains' (viz., coarse grains), oilseeds (viz., groundnut, rapeseed/ mustard, cottonseed, linseed, castorseed), oils thereof including vanaspati, all imported oilseeds and oils, sugar, gur and khandsari and cotton and kapas to 'other' (other than cotton mills including spinning mills) are subject to selective credit control stipulations.

In the context of the favourable supply situation, all the above mentioned commodities, except buffer stock and the unreleased stocks of sugar to sugar mills, are exempted from all the stipulations of selective credit control effective October 21, 1996. Banks are free to fix prudential margins on advances against sensitive commodities.

The minimum margin on unreleased stocks of sugar is being lowered by 5 percentage points from the existing 20 percent to 15 percent effective October 21, 1996. With this relaxation, the valuation of stocks of sugar will revert to the method that existed prior to July 1, 1996. In the case of buffer stock of sugar, the existing prescription of a zero percent would continue.
A communication on these changes is being issued to banks separately.
(h) Foreign Currency Denominated Loans

With a view to giving greater flexibility to borrowers engaged in productive activities of the economy, banks will be permitted to provide foreign currency denominated loans to their customers under which foreign exchange risk is borne by the borrowers for meeting either foreign currency or rupee requirments, subject to the following conditions:

(i) The resource base for such loans would consist of Foreign Currency Non-Resident Accounts (Banks) Scheme (FCNR(B)). Banks will not, however, be permitted to fund a foreign currency loans through a buy sell swap.
(ii) The purpose, tenor and interest rates on these loans may be decided by the banks, within the prudential framework and the credit monitoring guidelines in force.

(iii) Personal loans and loans for consumer durables, etc., should not be provided under this scheme, since the objective is to provide for genuine credit requirements of productive sectors in the economy.
Detailed operating instructions would be issued seperately.
(i) Consortium Lending

In cases of multiple lending, the threshold limit of working capital finance, for obligatory consortium arrangement, was raised from Rs. 5 crore to Rs. 50 crore in October 1993. Reserve Bank has also laid down guidelines for lending under consortium arrangement which has been formed either on a voluntary basis or on the basis of the mandate of the Reserve Bank.

While the threshold limit for obligatory consortium arrangement would continue to be Rs. 50 crore, it has been decided that whatever consortium is formed, either on a voluntary basis or on obligatory basis the ground rules of the consortium arrangement, viz. number of participating banks, minimum share of each bank, entry/exit from consortium, the grant of any facility to the borrower by a non-member bank, etc., will be framed by the participating banks in the consortium. In the case of existing consortia, the participating banks may undertake a review of the rules and may make such modifications as are considered necessary.
Detailed operating instructions are being issued to banks separately.
(j) Loans System for Delivery of Bank Credit

A 'loan system' introduced in April 1995, with a view to imparting an element of discipline in the utilisation of bank credit, has been extended in phases to cover larger number of borrowers with the percentage of the 'loan component' of the working capital limit being gradually enhanced. It has now been decided to effect the following further modification in the system:

(i) In the case of borrowers with assessed maximum permissible bank finance (MPBF) of Rs. 10 crore or above but less than Rs. 20 crore, the 'cash credit component' is restricted to 60 percent of the MPBF and the balance 40 percent is 'loan component'. The 'cash credit component' will now be restricted to 40 percent and the balance 60 percent would be in the form 'loan component'.
In order to impart greater flexibility and convenience to the borrowers, the following changes are being made in the 'loan system':
(i) The minimum period of 'loan component' would be six months as against one year at present.
(ii) The 'loan component' would henceforth be permitted to be renewed/rolled over.

(iii) 'Bill Limit' for inland sales would henceforth be permitted to be carved out of the 'loan component' in the case of all borrowers. Hitherto, this limit was required to be carved out of the 'cash credit component' except in cases of borrowers availing of export credit in excess of the permissible percentage of 'cash credit component'
(k) Commercial Paper

Commercial Paper (CP) can be issued by corporate customers, subject to the terms and conditions laid down in the 'Non-Banking Companies (Acceptance of Deposits through Commercial Paper) Direction, 1989' which require that the commercial paper issued would have to be reduced from Permissible Working Capital limit.

After introduction of the 'loan system', the amount of commercial paper is required to be carved out of the 'cash credit component' of the working capital limit. In view of the further reduction in the 'cash credit component', it has been decided that the amount of commercial paper that can be issued will not henceforth be restricted to the cash credit component'.
Detailed operating instructions are being issued separately.
(l) Banks' Investments in Shares and Debentures

Scheduled commercial banks are, at present, allowed to subscribe to shares and debentures in the primary market inclusive of devolvement through underwriting and investment in mutual funds, upto 5 percent of the incremental deposits of the previous year. Banks are, however, not allowed to purchase shares and debentures in the secondary market.
It has not been decided to allow banks to purchase shares and debentures in the secondary market within the existing ceiling of 5 percent of incremental deposits.
Detailed instructions are being issued seperately.
SUMMING UP

15. The overall effect of the above measures would be an expansion in the lendable resources of banks without fuelling excessive monetary expansion and inflation. The reduction in the CRR and the changed modalities for the use of FCNR (B) funds will not only augment the lendable resources but also bring about a reduction in the cost of credit.

However, the reduction in the CRR should not be viewed only as a response to certain short term devolvements. It is a part of the plan to bring about restructuring of the CRR - refinance regime through a simultaneous reduction in reserve requirement and refinance entitlements.

The changes proposed in the consortium arrangement, issue of commercial paper and cash credit-loan composition will impart greater flexibility to the credit delivery system. There has been a growing concern about the rise in the cost of credit. An enduring reduction in the interest rate can be brought about only if inflation rate remains at a resonably low level and the inflationary expectations are broken.
